content: Enteritis refers to the inflammation of the small intestine. If the inflammation involves the large intestine, it is termed colitis, while enterocolitis describes inflammation affecting both the small and large intestines. Symptoms of enteritis may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, abdominal distension, and hematochezia (the passage of fresh blood through the rectum). If vomiting is present, the condition is more accurately diagnosed as gastroenteritis. A thorough medical history is crucial in distinguishing serious cases of enteritis from those that are self-limiting. Key factors that may prompt further investigation include the presence of blood in the stool, signs of dehydration, skin eruptions, a suspected link to food exposure, or recent travel to areas where enteritis is endemic. Acute enteritis is most commonly caused by bacterial or viral infections. When food is implicated, foodborne illness should be suspected. If other members of the household or family are also affected, this may indicate an infectious etiology. Chronic enteritis, on the other hand, may result from conditions such as Crohn's disease, giardiasis, tuberculosis, celiac disease, or, in rare cases, Whipple's disease. Viral diarrhea associated with enteritis is typically self-limiting and managed with rehydration therapy. In cases where bacterial causes are suspected, such as after recent travel or food poisoning, antibiotics may be considered. Chronic forms of enteritis are treated based on the underlying diagnosis, with specific management tailored to the condition (e.g., Crohn's disease or celiac disease).
